To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) virtual human agents that tell their own stories (first person) are more engaging to the user than virtual human agents that relate the stories of humans they know (third person), but 2) the agent's honesty is not affected by the choice of first or third person.

(1) presenting stories about the agent’s own past life (i.e., first person perspective) increased users’ engagement, and (2) presenting stories about humans the agent knew (i.e., third person perspective) was not perceived as dishonest.

(1) virtual humans can use personal autobiographical stories in first person to engage users in long-term interactions; (2) users enjoy the interaction and are not offended by the first person presentation of the stories, even if they know they are fictional.

how to develop virtual humans that are engaging and believable to users, while maintaining ethical standards.
